steps.say: Picture a sealed bag of identical coins. You cannot open it to count them, but you can weigh it.

steps.pre: So in 24 g of carbon, the number of moles is:
steps.say: Chemists count atoms the exact same way, because atoms are far too small to see. One mole of carbon weighs 12 g.

That IS the method: moles = mass ÷ Mr. The Mr is simply the mass of one 'unit' (one mole), like the weight of one coin. You weigh a sample to count atoms you can never see. First, though, you work out the Mr by adding the Ar of every atom in the formula.

steps.say: Mr is the total of every atom's Ar. MgCl₂ is 1 magnesium (Ar 24) and 2 chlorines (Ar 35.5 each). The subscript 2 means two chlorines.

steps.hint: Add magnesium's Ar to the chlorine total.

steps.done: Same total, 95. That was the whole move: multiply by the subscript, then add.
steps.hint: Add every atom out in full.

steps.done: Mr of ammonium sulfate is 132. The bracket was the whole point: double what is inside first.
steps.hint: Add the bracket part to the SO₄ part.

method_card.content:
The mole is the 'bridge' between masses you can weigh and atoms you cannot see.

Mr calculation: List each element, multiply Ar by subscript, add up. H₂SO₄: (2×1) + 32 + (4×16) = 98.

Moles: moles = mass ÷ Mr. One mole has a mass in grams equal to Mr. One mole contains 6.0 × 10²³ particles.

Percentage by mass: (Ar × number of atoms ÷ Mr) × 100. Do not forget to multiply by 100.

Common pitfalls:

  • Not multiplying Ar by the subscript (e.g. treating H₂O as H + O instead of 2H + O)
  • Forgetting × 100 in the percentage calculation
  • Confusing open and closed systems when discussing mass changes
steps: Find Mr: add up all Ar values in the formula, multiplying each by its subscript
Moles = mass (g) ÷ Mr. Rearrange: mass = moles × Mr; Mr = mass ÷ moles
Percentage by mass = (Ar × number of that atom ÷ Mr) × 100
Conservation of mass: in a closed system, total mass of reactants = total mass of products
method_card.title: Relative Formula Mass and Moles

guided_steps.pre: Number of hydrogen atoms (from the subscript 2):

guided_steps.hint: The Mr goes on the bottom.

guided_steps.say: Rearrange moles = mass ÷ Mr into mass = moles × Mr. Moles = 0.5, Mr of water = 18.

guided_steps.done: Back to 0.5 mol, so 9 g is right.

bronze.display: Calculate Mr of NaOH. (Ar: Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)

guided_steps.say: Mr is the total of every atom's Ar. NaOH has one Na (23), one O (16) and one H (1). No subscripts.

guided_steps.done: Same answer, 40. Mr of NaOH is 40.
guided_steps.hint: Add the three Ar values in one go.
guided_steps.pre: Check by adding all three straight: 23 + 16 + 1 =

bronze.hint: One of each atom, no subscripts: 23 + 16 + 1.

misconceptions.message: NaOH has one of each atom: 23 + 16 + 1 = 40. Check no atom was left out.

bronze.display: How many moles are in 8 g of magnesium? (Ar of Mg = 24)

guided_steps.say: moles = mass ÷ Mr. Magnesium's Ar is 24, so one mole weighs 24 g. Mass here is 8 g.

guided_steps.hint: The molar mass, 24, goes on the bottom.

guided_steps.done: That is 7.92 g, close to 8 g once you allow for rounding, so 0.33 mol is right.

misconceptions.message: moles = mass ÷ Mr = 8 ÷ 24 = 0.33 mol. Dividing the other way (24 ÷ 8) gives 3, which is wrong.

problem_bank.bronze_description: One equation, values already in the right units: add up the Ar values, or use moles = mass ÷ Mr, and calculate straight through.

gold.display: Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in urea, CO(NH2)2. (Mr = 60, Ar: N = 14)

guided_steps.say: Percentage by mass = (mass of that element ÷ Mr) × 100. The subscript 2 outside the bracket in CO(NH₂)₂ means 2 nitrogen atoms.

guided_steps.hint: The 2 outside the bracket doubles the one N inside.

guided_steps.done: 46.7% of urea's mass is nitrogen, which is why it is a good fertiliser.

gold.hint: The subscript 2 outside the bracket gives 2 N atoms: (2×14 ÷ 60) × 100.

misconceptions.message: The subscript 2 outside the bracket doubles everything inside, so there are 2 nitrogen atoms in total.

gold.display: Calculate Mr of Ca(OH)2. (Ar: Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1)

guided_steps.say: Mr is the total of every atom's Ar. The subscript 2 outside the bracket doubles EVERYTHING inside: 2 O and 2 H, plus 1 Ca.

guided_steps.done: Same total, 74. Mr of Ca(OH)₂ is 74.
guided_steps.hint: Add every atom out in full.

gold.hint: The 2 outside the bracket doubles the O and the H: 40 + 2×(16+1).

misconceptions.message: The 2 outside the bracket multiplies BOTH the O and the H: 40 + 2×(16+1) = 74. Doubling only the H gives 40+16+2 = 58.
Ca(OH)2 = Ca + 2×(O+H) = 40 + 2×17 = 74. Ignoring the subscript entirely gives 40+16+1 = 57.

gold.display: 2.4 g of magnesium burns in air to form 4.0 g of magnesium oxide. Calculate the mass of oxygen that reacted.

guided_steps.say: Conservation of mass: in a closed reaction, total mass in = total mass out. The magnesium plus the oxygen that reacted must equal the magnesium oxide made.

guided_steps.hint: Read it straight from the question, 4.0 g.
guided_steps.pre: Mass of the product, magnesium oxide:

guided_steps.hint: Product mass minus the magnesium mass.
guided_steps.pre: Subtract the magnesium you started with: 4.0 − 2.4 =

guided_steps.done: Magnesium plus oxygen gives 4.0 g, the oxide mass, so 1.6 g of oxygen reacted.
guided_steps.hint: Add the magnesium and your oxygen answer.

gold.hint: Conservation of mass: oxygen = product − magnesium = 4.0 − 2.4.

misconceptions.message: Mass of oxygen = mass of product − mass of Mg = 4.0 − 2.4 = 1.6 g. Adding them gives 6.4 g, which is impossible.

gold.display: How many moles are in 2.4 g of magnesium? (Ar of Mg = 24)

guided_steps.say: moles = mass ÷ Mr. Magnesium's Ar is 24, so one mole weighs 24 g. Mass here is 2.4 g.

guided_steps.hint: The molar mass, 24, goes on the bottom.

guided_steps.done: Back to 2.4 g, so 0.1 mol is correct.

misconceptions.message: moles = mass ÷ Mr = 2.4 ÷ 24 = 0.1 mol. Dividing the other way (24 ÷ 2.4) gives 10, which is wrong.

silver.display: A sample contains 0.25 mol of CaCO3 (Mr = 100). Calculate the mass.

guided_steps.say: Rearrange moles = mass ÷ Mr into mass = moles × Mr. Moles = 0.25, Mr = 100.

guided_steps.done: Back to 0.25 mol, so 25 g is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide your mass by the Mr.

silver.hint: Rearrange to mass = moles × Mr, then 0.25 × 100.

misconceptions.message: mass = moles × Mr = 0.25 × 100 = 25 g. Dividing (100 ÷ 0.25) gives 400, the wrong way round.

silver.display: Calculate the percentage by mass of oxygen in CO2. (Mr = 44, Ar O = 16)

guided_steps.say: Percentage by mass = (mass of that element ÷ Mr) × 100. CO₂ has 2 oxygen atoms.

misconceptions.message: CO2 has 2 oxygen atoms: (2×16/44) × 100 = (32/44) × 100 = 72.7%. Counting only one O gives (16/44)×100 = 36.4%.

silver.display: 2.5 mol of NaOH (Mr = 40) is dissolved in water. Calculate the mass in grams.

guided_steps.say: Rearrange to mass = moles × Mr. Moles = 2.5, Mr = 40. The water is just the solvent, ignore it.

guided_steps.done: Back to 2.5 mol, so 100 g is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide your mass by the Mr.

misconceptions.message: mass = moles × Mr = 2.5 × 40 = 100 g. Dividing (40 ÷ 2.5) gives 16, the wrong way round.
